sections.title: 1. Cloud Deployment Models: Public cloud; private cloud: on-premise vs hosted; hybrid & cloud bursting; community cloud

slides.heading: Deployment Models Map

content.line: A cloud deployment model defines who owns the infrastructure, where it is hosted, and who has access to it.
Different organisations choose different deployment models based on their *control, security, scalability, and sharing requirements.*
Let’s explore the four major deployment models.
Public cloud: provider-owned, shared across tenants
Private cloud: dedicated, either on-premise or hosted
Hybrid cloud: private and public linked together
Community cloud: shared by organisations with common needs

slides.visual_guidance: Four boxes labelled Public, Private, Hybrid, Community arranged around a central 'Infrastructure Choice' node, arrows showing a spectrum from fully shared to fully dedicated.

slides.heading: Public Cloud

content.line: A public cloud is a cloud environment where a cloud provider owns and manages the infrastructure, and multiple customers use its resources over the internet.
Infrastructure owned and run entirely by the provider
Many tenants share hardware, isolated logically from each other
Capacity scales rapidly across resources pooled across customers
Best fit: variable workloads, fast launch, low compliance limits

slides.analogy: A shared cab is owned by the cab company; many riders book seats and pay only for the ride taken, never owning the vehicle — just as public cloud tenants share provider-owned servers and pay only for the capacity used.
slides.visual_guidance: One large building labelled 'Provider Data Centre' with multiple small logos (different companies) drawing from it over an internet cloud icon.

slides.heading: Private Cloud

content.line: Private cloud dedicates infrastructure to one organisation only, chosen when compliance, data residency or latency needs rule out shared public hardware.

rows: Full logical control, no physical access

slides.analogy: Building a house on owned land gives full control forever; renting a private bungalow built by a developer gives the same exclusivity without construction effort — just as on-premise private cloud means owned infrastructure, while hosted private cloud means dedicated but provider-managed infrastructure.
slides.visual_guidance: Split diagram: left shows a building icon inside an organisation's fence (on-premise); right shows the same dedicated building inside a provider's larger data centre fence (hosted).

slides.heading: Hybrid Cloud

content.line: Hybrid cloud links private and public infrastructure so workloads move between them, avoiding the need to size on-premise capacity for rare demand peaks.
Sudden overload bursts into public cloud capacity temporarily
Cloud bursting: automatic overflow triggered by demand thresholds
Example: AWS Outposts extends AWS infrastructure into on-premise sites

slides.analogy: A restaurant kitchen handles daily orders alone, but during a wedding rush it hires a banquet hall's ovens for the overflow and releases them once the rush ends — just as cloud bursting shifts excess load to public cloud only during demand spikes.
slides.visual_guidance: Two linked boxes, 'Private Infrastructure' and 'Public Cloud', with a dashed arrow labelled 'burst' flowing from private to public only when a load gauge crosses a threshold line.

slides.heading: Community Cloud

content.line: Community cloud is infrastructure shared by several organisations with common regulatory, security or mission needs, rather than opened to the general public.
Governance and compliance rules set jointly by member organisations
Cost split among fewer tenants than public, more than solo private
Example: AWS GovCloud (US), reserved for government agencies and partners
Typical users: government bodies, healthcare consortiums, research collaborations

slides.visual_guidance: One shared infrastructure block in the centre with several matching organisation icons (government, healthcare, research) connected to it, ringed off from the general public cloud.

slides.heading: Deployment Models Compared

content.line: Choosing a deployment model trades control for convenience: full ownership costs more effort, full sharing costs less control.

rows: Dedicated capacity without own data centre
Member organisations, or a third party

slides.visual_guidance: The five-row comparison table rendered full-width, with the 'Owned By' column colour-coded to visually reinforce the control-versus-sharing spectrum from slide one.

sections.title: 2. Multi-Cloud: Motivations: resilience, negotiation & regulation; operational cost of multiple platforms

slides.heading: Multi-Cloud Defined

content.line: Multi-cloud means running workloads across two or more independent public providers at once, unlike hybrid cloud, which mixes public with private infrastructure.
AWS handles general-purpose compute and storage workloads
Azure serves Microsoft-integrated enterprise applications
GCP powers data analytics and AI/ML pipelines

slides.analogy: Spreading savings across two different banks guards against one bank freezing withdrawals or raising fees — just as multi-cloud spreads workloads across providers so one outage or price hike does not stop operations.
slides.visual_guidance: Diagram: one company icon with three arrows branching to AWS, Azure and GCP logos, each labelled with a workload type.

slides.heading: Multi-Cloud Motivations

content.line: Three business pressures push organizations toward multiple providers even though it adds complexity.
Resilience: a second provider keeps services running during an outage
Negotiation leverage: comparing quotes across vendors avoids one-sided pricing
Regulation: in-country hosting or concentration-risk rules may require a compliant region or a second provider

slides.visual_guidance: Three labelled icons (shield, handshake, gavel) mapped to resilience, negotiation and regulation respectively.

slides.heading: Operational Overhead Cost

content.line: Multi-cloud earns its resilience and leverage at a real operational price: every added provider multiplies what must be learned, managed and paid for.
Separate consoles, APIs and billing dashboards per provider
Distinct certifications and skill sets needed for each platform's staff
Cross-cloud data transfer (egress) charges between providers
Duplicate monitoring, security and IAM policies to maintain

slides.visual_guidance: Table-style graphic: rows for Skills, Tooling, Billing, Security — each row showing duplicated icons across AWS/Azure/GCP columns.

sections.title: 3. Service Models: IaaS, PaaS & SaaS: what each provides & abstracts; representative services

slides.heading: Service Model Spectrum

content.line: The three service models share one technology stack; each shifts the line dividing provider-managed layers from customer-managed layers.Deployment models say where the infrastructure sits and who owns it; service models say what is abstracted. Any service model can run on any deployment model (e.g. private-cloud IaaS, public-cloud SaaS).

slides.visual_guidance: Horizontal stack bar split into four layers, shaded by owner colour for IaaS, PaaS and SaaS side by side.

slides.heading: IaaS Explained

content.line: Infrastructure as a Service rents compute, storage and network as raw building blocks, leaving the operating system and everything above it to the customer.
Abstracts physical hardware, racking and data-centre wiring
Customer installs OS, runtime, middleware and application
Representative services: AWS (Amazon Web Services) EC2, EBS, VPC
Azure Virtual Machines, GCP Compute Engine offer same layer

slides.analogy: Domino's kitchen space and oven are used, but the dough, sauce and toppings are supplied separately and the pizza is cooked from scratch — just as the IaaS provider manages only the physical infrastructure while the customer manages the operating system, runtime and application.
slides.visual_guidance: Icon of empty kitchen equipment (oven, gas line) labelled Infrastructure, with a chef bringing own recipe cards labelled OS, Runtime, App to bake the pizza.

slides.heading: PaaS Explained

content.line: Platform as a Service adds a managed operating system and runtime atop infrastructure, so the customer only builds, deploys and runs application code.
Abstracts OS patching, runtime setup and server scaling
Less control over OS-level tuning than IaaS allows
Representative services: AWS Elastic Beanstalk, AWS App Runner
Azure App Service, GCP App Engine offer same layer

slides.analogy: Domino's kitchen, oven and ready dough are already set up, so only assembling and baking the pizza on that setup remains — just as the PaaS provider manages infrastructure, operating system and runtime while the customer manages only the application.
slides.visual_guidance: Icon of ready kitchen setup labelled Platform, chef adding only dough labelled Application Code.

slides.heading: SaaS Explained

content.line: Software as a Service delivers a finished application; the provider manages every layer beneath it, leaving the customer only account setup and data.
Abstracts the entire stack below the application
Provider pushes feature updates automatically, no customer action
Representative services: Gmail/Google Workspace, Salesforce, Microsoft 365
Customer effort and control both fall sharply toward SaaS

slides.analogy: A ready-made pizza is ordered directly from Domino's with no kitchen work at all — just as SaaS provider manages the entire stack while the customer only uses the finished application.
slides.visual_guidance: Icon of a finished pizza box handed over, labelled Application, contrasted with the empty and ready kitchens from the IaaS and PaaS slides.

sections.title: 4. Beyond the Big Three: Function as a Service (FaaS) & serverless; AI/ML-as-a-Service; responsibility boundaries across models

slides.heading: Beyond The Big Three

content.line: Cloud service models did not stop at IaaS, PaaS and SaaS. Two further models push abstraction higher, changing what the provider manages and what the developer retains.
Function as a Service (FaaS): runs code per trigger, no visible server
Serverless: broader term covering FaaS plus managed databases and queues
AI/ML-as-a-Service: consumes pre-built AI and ML models via API
Both shift most infrastructure responsibility onto the cloud provider

slides.visual_guidance: Spectrum diagram: IaaS -> PaaS -> SaaS -> FaaS/Serverless -> AI/ML-as-a-Service, arrow showing rising abstraction and shrinking user responsibility.

slides.tr_title: Function As A Service And Serverless
slides.heading: FaaS And Serverless

content.line: Function as a Service (FaaS) runs a single function only when triggered, removing any need to provision or manage a server.
Triggers: HTTP request, scheduled timer, queue message, file upload
Scales automatically from zero to many parallel invocations
Billed per invocation and execution time, not idle time
Runs on AWS Lambda; cold start delay if idle first

slides.analogy: Booking a cab only when travel is needed and paying just for that ride, instead of owning an idle car, mirrors FaaS: code runs only on a trigger and billing counts only execution time.
slides.visual_guidance: Timeline: idle -> trigger event -> function instantiated -> executes -> torn down, labelled with AWS Lambda.

slides.heading: AI ML As Service

content.line: AI/ML-as-a-Service (Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning as a Service) exposes pre-trained vision, language and forecasting models through a plain API call.
Representative services: Amazon Rekognition, Comprehend (pre-built APIs)
Provider manages model training, GPUs (Graphics Processing Units) and hosting
User manages input data and API integration only
Used in vision, chatbots, fraud and forecasting

slides.analogy: Consulting a specialist doctor for one diagnosis instead of building a hospital, paying only for that consultation — just as AI/ML-as-a-Service delivers intelligence via API without building the model.
slides.visual_guidance: Icon flow: application -> API call -> pre-trained model service -> prediction returned, labelled Amazon SageMaker / Rekognition.

slides.heading: Full Responsibility Spectrum

content.line: Moving from IaaS toward SaaS steadily shifts management from user to provider; FaaS and AI/ML-as-a-Service remove the server concept, but the user still manages function code or input data respectively.

slides.visual_guidance: Full-width table, one row per model, shading intensity rising left to right to show growing provider responsibility.

sections.title: 5. Cloud Economics & Providers: CapEx vs OpEx; total cost of ownership (TCO); pricing: on-demand, committed use & spot; AWS, Azure, GCP & Indian providers

slides.heading: Cloud Economics Map

content.line: Cloud adoption decisions turn on how spending is structured and who supplies the infrastructure.
CapEx vs OpEx: how spend is classified
TCO: true multi-year cost of a choice
Pricing models: on-demand, committed use, spot
Providers: global hyperscalers and Indian regional players

slides.visual_guidance: Four-quadrant map, one label per quadrant: CapEx/OpEx, TCO, Pricing Models, Providers.

slides.tr_title: CapEx vs OpEx — The Accounting View
slides.heading: CapEx vs OpEx

content.line: Cloud does not just change how much is paid; it changes which financial statement absorbs the cost, reshaping approvals and tax treatment.
CapEx: capitalised, depreciated over asset life, sits on balance sheet
OpEx: expensed immediately, hits the income statement same period
CapEx typically needs board-level capital approval
OpEx approval sits within departmental budgets
Depreciation deductions (CapEx) shift tax timing versus OpEx's immediate deduction
AWS Cost and Usage Report classifies spend for finance systems

slides.analogy: Buying a house needs a large loan and years of EMIs recorded as an asset, while renting is a monthly expense with nothing recorded — just as CapEx locks value on the balance sheet while OpEx flows straight through the income statement.
slides.visual_guidance: Split panel: balance sheet with a depreciation curve versus income statement with a flat recurring expense line.

slides.heading: Total Cost Ownership

content.line: Total cost of ownership (TCO) totals every direct and indirect cost of running a workload across its life, not only the sticker price.
Direct costs: compute, storage, licensing, network transfer
Indirect costs: staffing, training, downtime, migration effort
On-premise adds power, cooling, floor space, hardware refresh
AWS Pricing Calculator estimates cloud cost.
Migration Evaluator builds the on-premise vs cloud business case

slides.analogy: A smartphone's price tag ignores the data plan, repairs and accessories bought over its life — just as a server's purchase price ignores the staffing, power and downtime that TCO adds back in.
slides.visual_guidance: Layered bar: sticker price at the base, staffing/power/downtime stacked above it to show true TCO.

slides.heading: Three Pricing Models

content.line: Providers meter usage but let buyers trade commitment for discount; three payment patterns cover most cloud spend.
On-demand: metered pay-as-used rate, zero commitment
Committed use: one to three-year term for lower fixed rate
Spot: spare capacity at a steep discount; can be reclaimed at short notice
Trade-off across all three: flexibility versus price

slides.analogy: A general train ticket costs full fare and needs no planning, a season pass costs less for a fixed daily route, and a standby ticket is cheapest but the seat can be given away — just as on-demand, committed use and spot trade flexibility for price.
slides.visual_guidance: Three tickets side by side, labelled On-Demand, Committed Use, Spot, with a price arrow decreasing left to right.

slides.heading: Pricing Models Compared

content.line: Each pricing model suits a different workload shape; committed-use discounts deepen with longer terms and more upfront payment.

rows: Highest unit price; cost runs on if left running
Reclaimed with short notice (~2 min AWS, ~30 sec Azure/GCP)

slides.visual_guidance: Three-column bar chart showing discount depth against flexibility surrendered for each model.

slides.heading: Global Cloud Providers

content.line: Three hyperscalers dominate global cloud spend, each with a different platform strength that shapes provider choice.

rows: Broadest service catalog, largest market share
Strong enterprise and hybrid integration (Active Directory)

slides.visual_guidance: Three logos in a row, one strength keyword under each.

slides.heading: Indian Cloud Providers

content.line: Alongside global hyperscalers, Indian providers compete on data residency, latency for local users, and rupee-denominated billing.
CtrlS, Yotta, E2E Networks: private data-centre players
Government's GI Cloud (MeghRaj) hosts public-sector workloads
BFSI and government workloads often mandate in-country storage
Regional providers can undercut hyperscaler pricing for local traffic

slides.visual_guidance: Map of India with data-centre pins beside the hyperscaler logos for scale comparison.
